documents: Carr, Carmichael & Pettit (2022), Wintertime brine discharge at the surface of a cold polar glacier and the unexpected absence of associated seismicity, JGR Earth Surface 127, e2021JF006325 (published PDF, 15 pages; supporting information not supplied)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (article pages '1 of 15' to '15 of 15', identical to PDF pages counted from 1)

entry.evidence: An unresolved question is what triggers the episodic brine release.

sequences.source_document: Carr et al. 2022, JGR Earth Surface, published PDF

steps.action: Pose the unresolved question of what triggers episodic brine release at Blood Falls.
steps.quote: An unresolved question is what triggers the episodic brine release.

steps.action: Take up the authors' earlier hypothesis (Carmichael et al. 2012, with two of the present authors) that meltwater-driven summer fracturing triggers brine outflow.
steps.quote: [...] . (2012) hypothesize that meltwater-driven fracturing during the summer melt season could propagate deep enough into the glacier

steps.action: Use historical springtime observations of brine icing on lake ice as indirect evidence of winter releases.
steps.quote: springtime observations of brine icing superimposed on lake ice (e.g., Black, 1969; Keys, 1979) indirectly suggest that brine releases can occur during the wintertime

steps.action: Set the meltwater hypothesis against the historical winter-release record and conclude it cannot explain all events.
steps.quote: This implies that meltwater-driven fracture cannot explain all brine release events.

steps.action: Report surface cracks tens of meters long and up to tens of centimeters wide seen after brine releases, including after the 2014 event (Figure S1).
steps.quote: Cracks in the glacier surface are often observed following a brine release event

steps.action: Take from published glacier seismology the expectation that surface crack opening generates Rayleigh waves.
steps.quote: Surface crack opening generates Rayleigh waves, a type of seismic surface wave, including in glacial settings

steps.action: State the test hypothesis: opening of Blood Falls cracks produces detectable, elevated Rayleigh-wave seismicity before and/or during the winter 2014 release.
steps.quote: we test the hypothesis that the opening of Blood Falls-related cracks at the glacier surface generates detectable Rayleigh waves with elevated seismicity

steps.action: Build a Rayleigh-wave correlation detector, modified from Chael (1997), that fixes the back azimuth to the known Blood Falls source and declares events with CFAR thresholds from best-fit normal densities per 30-min block.
steps.quote: We therefore developed a Rayleigh wave activity detector to monitor the Blood Falls source region

steps.action: Deploy a time-lapse camera and a 3-station L-22 seismometer network (one on ice, two on frozen sediment) from Nov 2013 to Jan 2015, which recorded the live winter 2014 event; exclude poor-quality data after spectrogram review.
steps.quote: We deployed a 3-seismometer network (Figure 2a).

steps.action: Document from time-lapse photos a pulsed winter brine release first visible on 13 May 2014 and continuing through at least 8 June, with later modification of the icing fan.
steps.quote: a time-lapse camera captured brine outflow activity as a series of pulsed events, first visible on 13 May

steps.action: Use nearby meteorological-station air temperatures (max −4.1°C, mean −20.7°C) to exclude surface-melt hydrofracture as the trigger of this event.
steps.quote: we therefore do not expect that any surface melt occurred.

steps.action: Compile Rayleigh event detection rates per 30 min at the three stations over the full record, showing a seasonal pattern with the highest rates in November-January.
steps.quote: We detect Rayleigh events during all times of the year, with the highest event detection rates in November–January.

steps.action: Run the detector at two CFAR thresholds (5e-5 and 5e-6), chosen by comparison with manually identified waveforms, and find the same relative patterns.
steps.quote: The same relative patterns of seismicity are apparent for both CFAR values.

steps.action: Estimate the minimum detectable crack size by injecting a Futterman-attenuated synthetic Rayleigh pulse into real noise samples and scaling it until it crosses each 30-min threshold, for 10-30 May 2014.
steps.quote: average 2.2 and 2.3 m, respectively, for land-based stations CECE and KRIS, and 2.9 m for on-ice station JESS

steps.action: Repeat the threshold estimate over 15 noise samples per window to give a range, and note that the land-versus-ice pattern matches the earlier STA/LTA results on the same data.
steps.quote: We tested 15 different noise samples per 30-min window.

steps.action: Compare release-period Rayleigh rates, durations, statistics and frequencies with the rest of winter and find no distinct signal: the hypothesis fails.
steps.quote: our seismic analysis shows no distinct seismic signal associated with this brine release.

steps.action: After the null result, pose four rival explanations: signal outside the frequency band, source too deep, sources below threshold or aseismic, or masking by environmental microseismicity.
steps.quote: (d) the sources are masked by myriad other environmental sources.

steps.action: Check the one possible exception, the 13 May JESS rate spike, against the other two stations, where it is absent.
steps.quote: The brief spike in event rate is not observed at the other stations.

steps.action: Exclude the frequency-band rival for surface crevassing by comparing the detector's band and duration limits with published crevasse Rayleigh-wave characteristics; basal stick-slip sources stay undetectable by design.
steps.quote: We therefore expect that if there are Rayleigh-wave generating surface crevassing events at our field site, our detector should find them

steps.action: Compute the source depth at which a crack-opening source would fall below detection, using the radiation pattern that maximizes displacement (Text S5).
steps.quote: We estimate that sources with depths around 2.5 km or deeper would evade detection

steps.action: Exclude the deep-source rival because glacier thickness at the terminus (tens of meters to 125 m) is far less than 2.5 km.
steps.quote: if basal crevasses excited Rayleigh wave energy, particularly in the shallow (<50 m) ice at the terminus, we would detect the events

steps.action: Compare the observed Blood Falls crack scale with the detection thresholds; repeated sub-threshold cracking stays possible and cannot be excluded.
steps.quote: We cannot exclude this possibility.

steps.action: Note an omitted auxiliary, attenuation in the englacial brine zone, which would raise thresholds and favour the sub-threshold rival.
steps.quote: if we were to, we expect the threshold crack edge length to be larger for sources within this zone of partially melted brine.

steps.action: Compare minimum detectable crack sizes with environmental crack sources (lake ice, ice-cored moraines, cliff collapse) and use the incoherence of rates between sensors to support masking.
steps.quote: have equivalent volumetric opening to cracks that are in the range of 2 m deep by 2 m long and opening 0.01 m.

steps.action: Propose that year-round thermally induced fracture of ice and frozen sediment, driven by temperature swings during wind events, plus summer meltwater hydrofracture, sets the background; the wind link is stated as untested.
steps.quote: We suggest that year-round small seismic sources emanate from thermally induced ice and frozen sediment

steps.action: Keep as best explanation a release model in which brine pressure drives basal crevassing and crack opening proceeds as many small events masked by background microseismicity.
steps.quote: We propose that the crack opening, both of basal crevasses and expansion of pre-existing surface crevasses, consists of a series of volumetrically small opening events

tree.answer: Episodic brine release at Blood Falls; a winter 2014 release documented by time-lapse
Release seen directly; fracturing only through Rayleigh-wave detection
Test whether crack opening gives elevated Rayleigh seismicity around release
Meltwater hydrofracture vs non-melt trigger; after the null, four rivals for the absence of a signal
Elevated rate expected vs none; deep source predicts detection loss only beyond ~2.5 km
Conditions found: one live winter 2014 event recorded by camera and three stations
Null holds at both CFARs; the 13 May spike does not replicate at the other stations
No discernible signal; meltwater and deep-source rivals excluded; sub-threshold and masking kept as best explanation

end.claim: The winter 2014 Blood Falls brine release occurred without surface melt and without discernible elevated Rayleigh-wave activity, rejecting the tested hypothesis; any associated fracturing is best explained as a series of small openings masked by environmental microseismicity.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing release-period Rayleigh detection rates at three stations with the rest of winter, using the known-source correlation detector, produced the null result on which the paper rests.

gates.evidence: The seismometers and camera were installed in Nov 2013, before the event and before the hypothesis was framed. The hypothesis was motivated by cracks seen in the following summer (p. 2), and it directed only the design of the detector and the reanalysis (p. 5). The hypothesis could have succeeded but failed (p. 10). The CFAR thresholds were 'subjectively determined' (p. 7), and nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Hilbert transform (π/2 phase advance) of the vertical channel to linearize Rayleigh-wave polarization
Constant false alarm rate (CFAR) thresholding of a detection statistic

imports.field: statistics (CTBT monitoring statistics, Wiechecki-Vergara et al. 2001)
imports.item: Large-sample normality of the correlation statistic used to set thresholds

novelty_claims.quote: In contrast, we assume a known source location (Blood Falls) and monitor the correlation values through time
The minimum detectable event size analysis is a robust tool that can be used to characterize detector sensitivity in other noisy seismic environments.

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: (1) the wintertime release was documented by photos (observation, not given a status); (2) surface-melt hydrofracture is excluded for this one event only, on temperatures from a station about 3 km up-glacier (excluded); (3) the minimum detectable crack edge lengths of 2.2-2.9 m are estimate_with_resolution, covering only three winter weeks, 15 noise samples per window, homogeneous Q, and with some windows above the 5.6 m tested maximum; (4) masking by microseismicity is best_explanation, and the wind/thermal driver is explicitly untested (p. 13). The result rests on one event (n = 1). The two CFAR values were chosen subjectively and the paper does not show the effect of other values. The detector's higher sensitivity than STA/LTA is asserted 'in principle', not measured. There is no ground-truth catalogue of the detector's false or missed detections beyond the statistical CFAR. Inferred, not stated: the network was deployed for broader MIDGE aims, and the Rayleigh hypothesis was framed after the event, once cracks were seen in summer 2014-15, so data acquisition was not hypothesis-directed. Three anonymous reviewers are acknowledged, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The supporting information (Texts S1-S6) was not supplied, so methods-only checks there cannot be verified. The trace_series composition fits only loosely: a single found event, three stations standing in for independent traces, and rivals for a null result rather than for a positive phenomenon. The novelty claims are implicit; there is no 'first' statement.

disagreements.target: Carmichael et al. (2012), meltwater-driven surface crevassing as the trigger of Blood Falls brine release
disagreements.support: Air temperatures stayed well below freezing during the winter 2014 release, and no Rayleigh signal of meltwater-driven fracture was found; the authors keep meltwater fracture for summertime seismicity.
disagreements.quote: This suggests that this particular brine release was not triggered by a surface meltwater drainage event

disagreements.target: STA/LTA detectors applied in the authors' previous study (Carr et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: Correlation-statistic detectors are argued, citing Carmichael & Nemzek (2019), to be more sensitive than incoherent-energy STA/LTA detectors; this is not quantified on these data.
disagreements.quote: our detector has, in principle, the capability to identify waveforms of lower energy

alternatives_considered.chosen: Correlation detector of elliptically polarized energy (modified Chael 1997)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Standard STA/LTA detector used in Carr et al. (2020)
alternatives_considered.reason: Correlation detectors are more sensitive to lower-energy waveforms

alternatives_considered.chosen: Fixed back azimuth toward the known Blood Falls source, monitored through time
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Scanning possible back azimuths to locate unknown sources
alternatives_considered.reason: The source location (Blood Falls) is known
Smaller CFARs skipped manually identifiable waveforms; larger CFARs flagged elliptically polarized noise (subjective compromise)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Homogeneous attenuation, Q = sqrt(35*45) (or 40), from Carmichael et al. (2015)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Including extra attenuation in the englacial brine zone imaged by radio echo sounding

alternatives_considered.chosen: Radiation pattern for crack opening toward the receiver
